How Coral Reefs Recover After Bleaching

Coral bleaching happens when water stays too warm for too long and corals expel the algae that live in their tissue and feed them. Without those algae the coral turns white and starts to starve.

A ten-year study of 120 reefs found that reefs with fewer than 3 bleaching events per decade recovered most of their coral cover within 9 to 12 years. Reefs that bleached more often did not recover.

Share on XShare on Facebook

What helps recovery

Researchers found three factors that speed recovery: good water quality, healthy populations of grazing fish that keep seaweed down, and nearby reefs that supply coral larvae.

Local actions such as reducing fertiliser runoff and limiting fishing of parrotfish improved recovery rates by about 30 percent in the study area.

Limits

The authors stress that local protection cannot replace cutting greenhouse gas emissions, because the time between heatwaves is getting shorter than the time reefs need to recover.
